
"Having raw records" means you must at least be able to trace back to the input and state which version that input belongs to and what was first displayed at the time. Without a version, you cannot use the values currently on the page to fill in the past; without the first result, you also cannot substitute a later successful rerun. Documenting the missing items is more useful than supplying a seemingly reasonable answer, because the next person taking over needs to know why the tree did not continue.

The most recent normal sample must also support comparison at the same point. Seeing only an adjacent directory, an aggregate value, or a screenshot without the input does not establish that the two samples match. If no comparable normal sample can be found, preserve the current abnormal sample and stop at "Cannot compare"; do not treat an average result as a normal sample.

## Handling Missing Records

When only a page prompt is available, record its location and the text currently visible, then collect the missing data. Prompts expire, so they only indicate where the investigation started when you took over, not what happened in the original incident. If an action would clear or overwrite state before the missing data is collected, do not perform that action yet.

When only directory names are visible, first confirm whether you can get back from the entry point to the original material for `license-quality-signal`. If not, stay on the entry-point branch. A directory name can be a clue for locating something, but it cannot by itself prove that the signal is stuck at a particular stage.

When only the final display remains, preserve it as the result the user ultimately saw and note that the original input is missing. The final display cannot be used to infer intermediate behavior retrospectively; once the raw records are available, restart from the main tree rather than retroactively recording the display as the input at the time.

When page access is restricted by permissions, record the entry point currently visible and the material that cannot be seen, then hand off to the permissions owner. Keep permission issues separate from issues with the quality signal itself: after read access is restored, reassess from the data collection branch rather than jumping directly to `route table`.

## Comparison Once Samples Are Available

When comparing the abnormal sample with the most recent normal `gateway event`, look only for the first difference. If the first difference is still unclear, do not explain the second one, much less infer the cause at the end of the chain. This avoids mixing input changes, environmental changes, and interface changes into a single handoff note.

When there is no difference at the first point, the next step is to check the environment or entry point. "Match" only means that no difference was found at the point compared, not that all behavior within the project has been verified. Do not close the record on the grounds of "no difference" at this point, and do not write it up as though permissions, indexes, or resources have already been ruled out.

When there is a difference at the first point, first ask whether it is still within LICENSE · Quality Signal Board. Resource, permission, or index issues still within the project go to the on-duty maintainer to continue checking at that point. Once a clearly defined interface has been crossed, stop this page's tree at `route table`, then hand off to the corresponding owner. If the location is unclear, return to the data collection branch; do not describe an ambiguous location as an interface boundary just to choose someone to take over.

## Replays and Retries

Before performing `opposite-input replay`, preserve the first failed sample and clearly document the single condition being changed this time. Do not replay if the condition cannot be stated clearly. After the replay, retain both the original failure and the new result, not just the green one.

If the replay is still stuck, return to the first difference rather than automatically treating a repeated failure as a new cause. If the replay turns green, this only shows that behavior after changing the input or environment differs from the original incident; it can narrow the branch, but cannot prove that the original incident has recovered. If the replay version differs from the version at the first failure, keep both versions side by side as well.

LAPIA-016 documented an issue with missing arguments in the original command. The complete command must be recovered separately, and the sample with missing arguments and the result after adding the arguments must be recorded separately. The result after adding the arguments cannot overwrite the first failure with missing arguments, nor can it be used to infer retrospectively that the entry point already included all arguments at the time.

## Navigation and Version Prompts

LAPIA-005 is a comparison entry point adjacent to the current revision. It can be used to find a working adjacent path and compare only the first path difference; results from the adjacent path must not be transplanted as results for the current entry point.

LAPIA-015 documents the version synchronization lag for adj-license. The page's entry-point prompt was at one point still pointing to an expiration action that was no longer valid, and later the entry-point prompt was changed back to pending update, with the invalid action no longer offered to newcomers to click. When you encounter an old prompt, retain it as a historical reference for locating the issue, but do not use it to determine the version or status of the current sample.

LAPIA-026 focuses on the navigation chain for the current revision. After actual consumers enter from the current revision, the first broken-link location should be recorded. Being able to open the entry point only establishes that the entry point is reachable; whether the subsequent path is usable must still be established from the first broken-link location.

## Handoff and Stopping

Branches that remain within the project are continued by the on-duty maintainer; every additional change in conditions is saved as a new sample. When the page is not visible, hand off to the permissions owner and state what is currently visible. When an interface has been crossed, stop at `route table` and provide the original sample location, version, first result, and first difference.

If further troubleshooting would change the user-visible contract, do not continue replays or experiments on this page, and open a separate formal review. This page is only responsible for routing the stuck behavior seen at the entry point to handling within the project, permission handling, or an interface handoff; without new evidence, the tree does not extend further downward.

# Quality Signal Troubleshooting Tree

When you see `license-quality-signal` stuck at the entry point, the most common mistake is not failing to find a possible cause, but attaching later results to the first failure too quickly. The person taking over should not start by guessing along familiar paths. First confirm whether the entry point left an original record; once there is a record, confirm whether it can be compared with the most recent known-good sample at the same point; only when the first difference falls within a clear boundary should you decide whether to keep it with LICENSE · Quality Signal Board, hand it to the permissions owner, or stop at the interface and hand it to the relevant owner.

This page is not for reverse-engineering the intermediate process from the final display. Each time, advance the tree only to the first point where new evidence is needed. When the incident material is incomplete, stop and mark what is missing; that is more reliable than filling in the gaps based on directory names, screenshots, or remembered call relationships. Rerunning, replaying, and fixing the page prompt may all be useful, but each can address only its own branch.

## First check what the entry point left behind when taking over

The entry point is in `docs/adj-license/runbooks/license-quality-signal-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`. After opening it, first look for the raw input rather than reading conclusions that have already beenorganized. At a minimum, leave the following side by side: the location of the raw input, the version it belongs to, the first result observed, and the environmental differences that could already be identified at the time. If any item is missing, you may continue logging it, but you cannot pretend that the sample is already comparable.

Early records used `request-local state` as the first place to look. This location is still worth checking first, but it is only the lookup target at the entry point, not a confirmed root cause. When the old incident was reviewed later, it became clear that if the raw material had not been fully retained, continuing to trace downward would connect remembered call relationships to blank spaces. Therefore, first ask "Which original record can we get back to?", and only then ask what the state in that record means.

The directory name, average value, and final display on the page serve different purposes. The directory name helps locate the entry point; the average value may show that some results were aggregated later; the final display shows what the user ultimately saw. None of the three can replace the first failed sample. If only one of them remains, preserve it as visible material first, then follow the collection branch; do not rewrite it as the input or intermediate result from that time.

The entry-point prompt must also be considered separately from the sample. The entry-point prompt is the note on the page telling people to continue looking for materials, and it may already be outdated; the sample is what was actually left behind after a run occurred. If the prompt is wrong, fixing the prompt is a maintenance action and does not mean that the quality signal has been confirmed to show the same type of fault. Conversely, a correct prompt does not mean that the subsequent path or the original record is necessarily still usable.

## Use this tree to locate the issue first; do not skip levels

```text
Can the current entry point provide the raw record?
├─ No
│  ├─ Only an entry-point prompt, directory name, or final display
│  │  └─ Record the visible location and content, then collect the missing data
│  └─ Page access is restricted
│     └─ Hand off to the permissions owner; do not infer a root cause from something being invisible
└─ Yes
   └─ Can you confirm the version and the first result observed?
      ├─ No
      │  └─ Stop at the collection branch and fill in missing items
      └─ Yes
         └─ Is there a recent normal gateway event to compare?
            ├─ No
            │  └─ Keep the anomalous sample; stop at "cannot compare"
            └─ Yes
               └─ Compare only the first difference
                  ├─ Same: check the environment or entry point
                  └─ Different
                     ├─ Still within the quality signal dashboard: the on-duty maintainer continues
                     └─ Crosses a clearly defined interface: stop at the route table and hand off to the corresponding owner
```

The tree's "raw record exists" does not mean "someone wrote a description." It must trace back to the input, identify which entry point it belongs to, and show the first result. If the raw input exists but the version is unclear, the sample is still incomplete; if the version exists but the first result was overwritten by a later green result, return to the collection branch. Do not replace the version from when the failure occurred with the version value currently shown on the page.

The tree's "recent normal sample" is also not just any green result. It must be comparable with the anomalous sample at the same location. An adjacent directory, a single aggregate value, a screenshot with no input, or a note that only says "normal later" cannot substitute for a normal sample. If no comparable sample can be found, the current anomalous sample still has value, but it can only stop the tree at "cannot compare"; it cannot hand the issue directly to a particular interface.

## When There Is No Raw Record

### Only the Page Prompt Remains

A page prompt can tell the person taking over where to start looking, but it cannot close any failure branch. Record the text currently visible and the page location, then collect the missing data. Before collecting missing data, first check whether the action will clear, overwrite, or change the current state; if it will change the state, do not retry yet. A green result produced before the original input was saved can only be treated as a new result; it cannot replace the original state.

If the object pointed to by the prompt no longer exists, keep the old prompt as a historical locator and record the point at which the current entry point can no longer proceed. Do not change the old prompt to a new path just to make the tree look complete, and do not infer from the old prompt which layer the anomaly must have occurred at. The current branch needs the raw record, not a path name that merely looks reasonable.

### Only a Directory Name

A directory name is not a record. First confirm whether you can get from the current entry point back to the raw materials for `license-quality-signal`. If you can, re-enter the main tree; if not, stop at the entry branch. A directory name can serve as a clue for the next search, but it cannot prove that the signal is stuck at a known stage, much less prove that an owner has taken over.

If the directory can still be opened but contains no input, version, or first result, still treat it as a missing record. Do not write "directory visible" as "materials available." Adjacent paths outside the directory can help locate the position, but results from adjacent paths must not be moved into the current sample.

### Only the final display remains

Retain the final display as a result sample. It shows what the user ultimately saw at that time; it does not show how the initial input entered, at which step it changed, or whether there were different intermediate results. Record the display together with "original input missing"; when the original materials are obtained later, reassess instead of back-writing the display as a request or event.

Be especially careful when the final display turns green. It may be the result of a later run, or it may come from a different condition; until it can be matched to the first failed sample, do not conclude from it that the environment has recovered. Green belongs only to the result seen that time; it does not cover the earlier failure for which a complete record was not saved.

### Page restricted by permissions

When the page cannot see the original materials, hand off to the permissions owner and state which parts of the entry are currently visible and which parts are not. Do not write "cannot see" as "did not happen," and do not write the permissions owner as a confirmed business root cause. After permissions are restored, restart from the collection branch and first verify the original input, version, and first result.

The permissions issue and the internal quality-signal issue can exist simultaneously, but the current page does not combine them. If the original record has not yet been seen, only reading permissions and entry reachability can be handled; this cannot determine whether the signal is stuck within the project or has already crossed the interface.

## The record exists, but the sample cannot yet be compared

Once the original record exists, first check whether both the version and the first result are present. The purpose of the version is to fix the record to a single entry state; the purpose of the first result is to preserve the initial behavior seen at that time. If either field is missing, do not fill it with later page content. You may record "version unknown" or "first result missing," but do not copy the current value just because you do not want to leave it blank.

If the versions differ, first write the version difference side by side. A version difference may explain the different behavior, or it may simply be a natural difference between two adjacent records; without the first path difference, do not directly write the version difference as the attribution. A comparison of the adjacent current revisions in LAPIA-005 can help find an adjacent position that can be traversed successfully, but it does not replace the current entry for comparison.

When the most recent normal sample cannot be found, do not substitute an average, an earlier directory screenshot, or a consolidated green conclusion. Retain the current abnormal sample, note that no comparable normal sample is available, and stop the tree at "cannot compare." You may continue looking for materials at this point, but the current record must not assume that the environment, entry, or interface has already been ruled out.

If a normal sample exists but it cannot be confirmed to come from the same position, still treat it as impossible to compare. Comparison is not placing two results that look similar side by side; it is confirming that the first difference can be sought at the same position. When the position is unclear, first add the entry and version information to avoid mixing phenomena from different stages into a single branch item.

## The first difference of `gateway event`

When comparison is possible, compare only the first difference with the most recent normal `gateway event`. If the earliest differing position has not been confirmed, do not explain the second or third difference, and do not infer the full call chain backward from the end symptom. This is not intended to simplify the anomaly into a single cause, but to let the person taking over know how far the current observation extends and where new evidence is needed.

When there is no difference at the first point, follow "Check the environment or entry point". Here, "match" only means that no difference was found at the positions compared; it does not mean that all resources, permissions, and indexes in the quality signal dashboard are functioning normally. Do not write "match" as "already ruled out", and do not delete the first failed sample just because there is no difference.

When the first difference appears, first determine whether it is still within LICENSE · Quality Signal Board. If the difference is still inside the project, hand it to the on-duty maintainer to continue checking from the current position. Do not pursue several possible causes at the same time; keep a separate sample for every operation that changes a condition, and distinguish it from the first failed sample.

When the first difference crosses a clearly defined interface, stop at `route table`. This is the handoff point, not a place to continue tracing the full call relationship on this page. When handing it to the corresponding owner, include the current entry point, original sample location, version, initial result, and first difference. If any one of these is missing, return to the collection or comparison branch; do not invent a boundary just to complete the handoff.

If the difference position cannot be clearly stated, the tree does not select an owner. Return to the collection branch and confirm the input, version, initial result, and comparison position. An ambiguous position is neither an interface boundary nor an attribution inside the project; it only indicates that the current record is insufficient to continue routing.

## Environment and entry-point branch

When the anomalous and normal samples match at the comparison point, check the environment or entry point next. First verify the saved environmental differences and entry-point visibility; do not extrapolate a complete cause from "samples match". Environmental differences are only part of the current situation; if they were not retained together with the first failed sample, they cannot be added later from memory.

The entry point itself may open and display the correct message, yet break in a later path. LAPIA-026 records the navigation-chain issue for the current revision: after the actual consumer enters through the current revision, record the first broken-link position. The fact that the entry point can open only shows that the entry point is reachable; it does not mean that the subsequent path works. Until the first broken link has been recorded, stop in the navigation branch.

For entry-point messages and version messages, preserve the distinction between "how the page was worded at the time" and "how the current page is worded". If the two differ, first correct the maintenance entry point or continue investigating navigation, but do not describe a change in the page text as the sample itself having changed. Samples, entry-point messages, and navigation paths are three different types of evidence.

## Conditions for using `opposite-input replay`

An old record contains an instance of retrying too early: the first failed sample had not yet been locked down when the next run began. What remained afterward was the green result from the rerun, making it difficult to determine the original state. Now preserve the first failed sample and environmental differences before considering `opposite-input replay`. This old lesson is kept here to prevent replay results from overwriting the earliest failure.

Before replaying, clearly state the single condition being changed this time. If the condition cannot be clearly stated, do not replay yet; results obtained after changing the input, version, and entry point at the same time cannot be used to locate the first difference. A replay is not meant to prove "it has already recovered", but to allow the two results to be saved side by side as evidence from different conditions.

After replaying, retain both the original failure and the new result, and label each with its version and first visible result. Do not delete the failure just because the new result turns green, and do not directly promote a repeated failure to a new root cause just because things are still blocked. The new result only shows that behavior differs or remains the same after a condition changes; the next step is still to return to the first difference in the main tree.

If the replay turns green, the precise conclusion is: after the input or environment changed, the behavior differed from what was observed in the original setting. This can narrow the scope of further investigation, but it cannot prove that recovery has occurred in the original setting. If the replay result looks the same as a normal sample, you still need to confirm whether the first difference lies within the project or is already beyond the interface.

LAPIA-016 are a reminder that missing parameters in the original command are also part of the history here. The complete command must be recovered separately; keep the failure sample from when parameters were missing separate from the result after the parameters were added. The result after the parameters were added must not overwrite the first failure from when parameters were missing, nor may it be treated as proof that the entry point had already executed the complete command at that time.

## Outdated prompts, revision, and adjacent paths

LAPIA-015 recorded a version synchronization lag for adj-license. For a time, the entry-point prompt on the page still pointed to an invalid expiration action; later, the entry-point prompt was changed back to pending update, and the invalid action was no longer available for newcomers to click. Changes like these show that page maintenance and samples from the original setting need to be handled separately: outdated prompts can be retained as historical reference points, but should no longer serve as operational entry points for people newly taking over.

When you encounter an outdated prompt, first record what it still points to, then record what the current page displays. Do not replace the old record with the current prompt, and do not treat the outdated prompt as a fact about the current revision. If an outdated prompt makes the entry point unusable, record the first broken link and enter the navigation or permissions branch if necessary, rather than calling the prompt itself the root cause of the quality signal.

The current revision comparison for adjacent paths in LAPIA-005 is also only used to find an entry point for comparison. An adjacent path can provide a working reference route, but its expiration action, entry-point prompt, environmental differences, and results must not be carried over to the current project. The current branch still needs to obtain its own raw input from the current entry point, then compare the first difference in the paths.

When an adjacent path already works but the current entry point is broken, record the first broken link at the current entry point, and do not use the adjacent path to bypass the broken link and continue troubleshooting. Materials from adjacent paths help indicate "where a comparison can be made", but do not replace evidence from the current entry point.

## Stay within the project, switch to permissions, or switch to the interface

If the first difference still involves LICENSE · Quality Signal Board's own resources, permissions, or indexes, stay within the project and have the on-duty maintainer continue checking. Further actions should still follow the current branch. For each additional condition change, save a new sample separately; do not write a later result back into the first failure sample.

When the original records cannot be viewed on the page, handle this as a permissions issue. When handing off to the permissions owner, state what is currently visible, what is missing, and where in the collection process the tree has stopped. After permissions are restored, start again from the entry point, without skipping the version and first result or replacing the original state with the page content shown after permissions are restored.

If the first difference has already crossed a clearly defined interface, stop at `route table`. The relevant owner only takes over the portion at their own interface; this page does not fill in call chains for adjacent projects or include unconfirmed downstream symptoms in the handoff. The handoff materials include only the samples and differences already saved, not causes inferred from directory names or the final displayed output.

If further action would change the user-visible contract, stop replays and experiments within the tree on this page, and initiate a separate formal review. This stopping point does not mean a decision has been made about how to change the contract, only that the triage page will not handle that decision any further. Preserving the state and defining a clear stopping point is more important than offering a solution here without comparing it.

## Where to go back if you take the wrong path

If a retry has already been attempted but the first failed sample is still available, return to the main tree and reassess using the first failed sample. The latest result must not become the only record of the state. Retain green results or new stuck states after a retry as additional samples, alongside the original failure.

If the first sample has already been cleared, this page cannot recover it. Record "First sample missing" and return to the collection branch; screenshots, directory names, and the remembered `gateway event` can only be treated as currently visible material, not used to stand in for the original input. At this point, do not continue explaining `route table` or the interface boundaries.

If you checked `route table` first and only then discovered that the original records were missing, return to the entry branch. You may retain the table entries already seen, but they must not be used to invent a first difference. If you have already handed off to the shared owner and only then discover that the difference is still within the project, return handling to the project, and explain that the redirection is because the boundary assessment has not yet been established; the incorrect routing is not itself the root cause.

If the page's entry point has been updated, retain the old link as a historical reference, but stop giving it to newcomers as an operational entry point. In LAPIA-015, setting invalidated due actions back to pending update is precisely how page corrections are kept separate from sample troubleshooting. After the page is fixed, you must still reassess based on the original records, version, and first result.

## A branching step can be recorded like this

Leave missing fields blank, and do not fill them in from memory:

```text
Entry point:
Original record location:
Version:
First observed result:
Environment differences visible at the time:
Most recent normal sample:
First difference:
Current branch:
Next step or stopping point:
```

When there are no original records, leave `Original record location` blank, and attach the currently visible entry-point hints, directory names, or final displayed output separately alongside it. Likewise, leave fields missing if the version is unknown, a normal sample is missing, or the location of the difference is unclear. The purpose of the record is not to disguise blank fields as conclusions, but to let the person taking over know where the next action should start and whether that action will change the state.

When deciding to perform `opposite-input replay`, specify the single condition being changed in addition to these lines, and put the new result in a separate entry. Do not put the replay result in the row for the first failure, since the two samples are records from different conditions.

## Related entry points

LAPIA-005: Comparison of adjacent current revision paths. Used to find an adjacent path that can be traversed, and compare only the first difference between paths.

LAPIA-015: adj-license version synchronization lag. The page entry-point hint was once out of sync with the nonfunctional expiration action, and the entry-point hint was later changed back to pending update.

LAPIA-016: The original command for the investigation branch was missing parameters. The complete command, the state with missing parameters and the results after adding the parameters are retained separately.

LAPIA-026: The current revision navigation chain is broken. Have an actual consumer enter from the current revision, and record the location of the first broken link.

These cards only help locate adjacent cases or maintenance entry points. When returning to this project, still start from the current entry point for `docs/adj-license/runbooks/license-quality-signal-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`, and proceed based on the original records, comparable samples and the first difference. Without new evidence, the tree stops at the current branch.

# Field notes on unresolved quality signals

I'm using this page to hold onto an awkward case from the quality signal dashboard. Failing samples had no fixed place in the regression tiers: sometimes they were treated as signals to revisit, and sometimes they were set aside as isolated fluctuations. At the time, I attributed those fluctuations to `test`, and only later learned that this was a misattribution. The original notes didn't retain any excerpts to support that judgment, and I didn't go back and fill in a full explanation of the cause; what this page preserves is that I got it wrong at the time.

The original timestamp for `revision` is still with the case materials; I haven't copied it onto this page. The unanswered status hasn't changed either: no one followed up with an answer about why the samples moved back and forth between tiers; the provisional note "don't count this as converged yet" was just my judgment when I stopped writing. It may no longer apply to later signals, but it explains why I didn't write that things had recovered at the time.

It used to be easy here to conflate "no reply" with "no problem." They aren't the same: the former only means this page is still waiting, while the latter needs support from additional samples. Since no reply came, I didn't adjust the initial classification any further, and I didn't remove the trace of that mistake.

The failing samples aren't listed one by one on this page, and the boundaries between regression tiers haven't been turned into rules either. I've only matched up the quality signal dashboard with those unstable signals; as you continue reviewing, log records that appeared later separately rather than folding them back into this misattribution. # Postmortem: dual-state anomaly in the response dependency

This records the case on response-egress-supply-boundary where the same object was left with two states. The object was originally maintained according to the dependency source, adoption scope, and exit responsibilities established based on the license, with its own schedule, maintainer, and exit conditions. The issue was not a change to the object's name: at two points in time, the current entry point showed different current revisions; both looked like records that could still be used.

The consumer compile probe exposed the issue first. Its result did not match the old record; at first, this was treated as a difference in the probe environment. Further comparison showed that the terminal state in the old record could not be reconciled with the state at the current entry point: one could reach the terminal handler, while the other still left the lifecycle promise change at an intermediate stage. Without the original command arguments, this was not enough to determine whether these were different stages of the same execution or two states written into the same object on separate occasions.

## Sequence of events

- After the first probe showed a mismatch, the old record was not immediately rewritten. The old page still retained the state observed at the time, to avoid overwriting the earlier output with the later output.
- Next, the version of `docs/adj-response-egress/incidents/Response-serialization-and-helpers-dependency-boundary-audit-two-states-for-one-object.md` from that time was saved, and further retries were stopped. Repeated runs did not recover the missing arguments; they would only make the final output line look more complete than what was observed at the time.
- When retracing from the original input, confirmation went only as far as the current entry point. It was noted that the terminal handler could be restored, but that only showed that a local path was reachable again; it did not support a conclusion about the lifecycle promise change.

Adoption scope and exit responsibilities cannot yet be determined from the entry page alone. The dependency source remains as originally recorded, and the exit action was not declared complete in this incident; describing the terminal handler's recovery as recovery of the whole object would hide the still-unexplained differences between the two states.

The working assessment at the time was that the navigation for the current revision and the old record did not provide a single reliable path; the consumer compile probe only proved that the two were inconsistent. The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause were kept together. # R30 Compatibility Window Decision Record

The initial draft framed the issue with R30 as "leave the entry point unchanged for now and wait for more samples". This sentence preserved the decision, but not the reasons for rejecting the other option at the time. In retrospect, it is also easy to read it as a stronger judgment than was actually made: as though request-ingress had already been proven to have no compatibility issues. The initial draft reached no such conclusion.

What was observed at the time was response; what was proposed was that it might indicate that request-ingress was no longer compatible. The two were closely linked in the meeting, so the earliest discussion put them in the same sentence. The ruling for R30 first separated that sentence: response was the observation, and a change in request-ingress was the explanation. An observation can trigger an investigation, but an explanation cannot directly become a window adjustment before it has been reproduced.

This record retains that earlier judgment because it shows the actual pressures behind this round's decision. If the window remained unchanged, users could not infer from "the entry point remains unchanged" that every gateway event was the same; if the window changed first, subsequent materials would in turn treat that action as a confirmed compatibility position. The review was not choosing between "there is a risk" and "there is no risk", but between two formulations that were still incomplete.

## The Two Options on the Table at the Time

The first option was to retain the current request-ingress entry point. It allowed response to continue to be recorded, explanations about the entry point to be proposed, and those explanations to be refuted later with counterexamples; R30 simply would not modify the compatibility window based on an observation that had not yet been aligned. With the entry point left unchanged, the scope already covered would continue to be handled under the existing position, and the window would not be used to extend a public surface commitment to uncovered scope.

The second option was to adjust the compatibility window. The supporters' concerns were substantial: if the differences in response ultimately did affect entry point semantics, narrowing the window earlier would seem more cautious and could also prevent ambiguous statements later. Nor was the objection that "the window cannot be adjusted". The objection was to letting a window action stand in for attribution before a reproduction linked response to request-ingress.

The decision was to take the first option and leave the window unchanged for now. This was a local decision, not a permanent definition. It did not determine the source of response or the outcomes for every gateway event, much less stipulate in advance that the entry point could never change. It only limited what R30 could approve at the time: the parts covered by existing evidence would be maintained; explanations not yet reproduced would not be incorporated into public-facing actions.

The wording "more samples" in the initial draft needs to be retained and corrected here. It looks like a general wait-and-see approach, but actually points to a very narrow prerequisite: first bring one specific event together with one fixed state. Without this prerequisite, adding more unrelated phenomena would only expand the vocabulary of the discussion, not make the compatibility rule clearer.

## Supplemental Review Notes

The supplemental review did not turn the old observation into a confirmed fault, nor did it project behavior that might have existed later back onto R30. The retrospective still started with request.js and the names request, response, and event. This was only to put the objects under discussion back into the same frozen repository state; filenames provided places to look, not proof of a compatibility boundary.

This was not clear enough in the initial draft. If someone inferred from the proximity of request.js that response must have been caused by the entry point, that conclusion would go even further than the original conjecture. Conversely, saying that the observed response was inconsequential because the entry point had not changed would also go beyond the materials available at the time. Paths help with rechecking, not as a substitute for reproduction.

The requirement left in the meeting materials was: `separate an observed response from the proposed explanation`. The separation here was not intended to turn every discussion into a lengthy record, but to require that a compatibility claim could at least be split into two sentences. The first sentence states what response was observed; the second states our guess as to why it occurred. The second sentence can stand as a working hypothesis, but it cannot pass itself off as the first sentence or trigger a public surface change on its own.

Another requirement was: `Reproduce one gateway event against one frozen repository state before proposing a compatibility rule or changing a public surface.` This threshold was deliberately not written as a declaration covering every event form. What R30 lacked at the time was not a broad glossary, but a reproduction that could bring the observation, object, and state together. Filling that gap first was more useful than making the window wording stricter.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["observed response"] --> C["Reproduce one gateway event"]
    B["proposed explanation"] --> C
    C --> D["one frozen repository state"]
    D --> E["compatibility rule or public surface"]
```

The connections in the diagram represent the review sequence, not that response and explanation have been proven to be the same thing. They are precisely the two sides that need to be kept separate. Only once a reproduction is tied to one gateway event and one frozen repository state is it permissible to discuss whether to propose a compatibility rule, or whether to change the public surface.

## Two Kinds of Cost

The cost of retaining the entry point was that the issue could not be closed out in a single sentence. There would still be readers within the window who wanted a judgment covering every gateway event, and this record could not provide one. That was not an omitted guarantee; there was no material at the time to support that breadth of coverage. Leaving the entry point unchanged simply avoided prematurely turning an explanation that had not yet been aligned into a long-term position.

The cost of adjusting the window was easier to overlook. Once the window moved, callers, explanatory materials, and subsequent reviews would naturally interpret that action as meaning that a compatibility judgment had been established. If a later reproduction overturned the original explanation, what needed to be withdrawn would include not just an implementation choice but also the external expectations that had already formed. R30 chose to bear the first cost.

The review retained the view that "narrowing the window first makes it easier to explain the risk". It pointed out that an unchanged entry point could not be read as a blanket guarantee; users might still encounter unexplained response. This view was not deleted as an error, because it described the real cost of retaining the status quo. The only reason it was not adopted was that describing risk cannot replace attribution.

Another reservation was whether one gateway event would be too narrow. If the goal was a complete compatibility statement, the answer was yes; one reproduction was not enough to cover all possible events. But the issue for R30 was not to write the entire compatibility statement in one go, but to determine whether the public surface could be changed for this window. For that action, first making one event recheckable in one fixed state was more appropriate than proceeding directly from an explanation that had not been separated out.

At the time, some also wanted to use response as the window switch in every case. This approach was not adopted. Any response that looked different could have come from several nearby objects; if it directly triggered a window change, the team would have an action first and then work backward to find a reason. It was exactly this sequence that R30 sought to avoid.

## Corrections to the Initial Draft

"Leave it unchanged for now" in the initial draft should be read as a decision on action, not as a technical attribution. It retained the current request-ingress, leaving the compatibility window unchanged for now; it did not conclude that response had been explained, or that response was unrelated to the entry point. If subsequent materials provide a reproduction of the same event in a fixed state, the old explanation should first be checked, and only then should it be decided whether the window judgment still applies.

Therefore, the decision for R30 can be reduced to three points: do not change the entry point based on an isolated response observation; do not write a proposed explanation as an observation; before proposing a compatibility rule or changing the public surface, first complete the required single-event, single-state reproduction. The third point is an approval threshold, not a final way to handle all compatibility issues.

This page still reflects the limitations of that earlier point in time. It is not a general guide for subsequent request-ingress work, nor does it define compatibility rules for other paths. Later readers who extract only "the entry point remains unchanged" will miss the reproduction conditions attached to that statement at the time; those who extract only "there are differences in response" will instead misread an unconfirmed explanation as a decision.

For the switchover handoff for consumer compile sweep, see DOC-44. The two efforts took place in the same phase, but the compile handoff is not evidence for retaining request-ingress, nor can it replace reproduction of a gateway event. Recording them separately is intended to prevent handoff progress from being mistaken for compatibility attribution in retrospect.

Two questions remain in the margin: whether the observed response ultimately crossed the request-ingress boundary; whether there is another category of gateway event that would invalidate this ruling to retain the entry point. No answers that might only become available later are added here. Material that could reopen this decision should first satisfy the reproduction method specified at the time, then explain which explanation or window judgment it changes.

# Code-reading notes: gateway replay entry point

When picking up this path, don't start by browsing through a string of similarly named files. First use `request-ingress` to locate where requests enter, then return to `request.js` and look only at the small section around `request` and `header` where the connections can be traced. The task here isn't to catalog every object with the same name, but to find an actual relationship from the public entry point that you can explain step by step.

The path sketch recorded at the time was:

```text
request-ingress
      |
      v
request.js: request / header entry points
      |
      v
one direct caller
      |
      v
first actual consumer of gateway replay rotation
```

`request.js` is the starting point for this review. First inspect where the request enters and where the header is handled within the same local section. Confirm that what you've found is request information near the entry point, rather than jumping elsewhere just because a search result matched a word. Record the entry-point object, the name of the call that leads from the entry point to the next stop, and where that call lands; copying only the matching lines for `request` or `header` doesn't show that you've traced the path any further.

`header envelope capture` serves as a location anchor in this search. When you see this marker, you can treat it as a point adjacent to where request information is being organized, then look back at the entry-point relationships before and after it. It helps the person picking this up tell that they're still on the request-ingress side, but it isn't the name of a gateway replay rotation consumer, and it can't connect the two path segments on its own. When recording it, explain its role as a location reference; don't promote it to a new processing stage.

When continuing from the entry point, follow only one direct caller. First, in the local section of `request.js`, find the call that hands off from the entry point to the next location, then verify that the call actually uses that next location. Don't list every location containing request/header side by side, or choose the "next file" in directory order. If the call name can be tied to a specific usage site, record this hop as entry point to direct caller; if all you have left is text with the same name, stay at this hop. A search hit cannot be treated as a call relationship.

Next, look for the first actual consumer of gateway replay rotation. "First" is determined by the direct relationships downstream of request-ingress, not by file-list order or name sorting. You're looking for an actual usage site that both links back to the call relationship in the previous step and shows where rotation starts being consumed on this path. Once you find it, record just the adjacent relationships between the entry point, the direct caller, and this usage site; there's no need to lay out all the internal processing that follows rotation.

Files with the same name but no call edge are still useful, just for a different purpose. They can prompt the person investigating to check another location, and help explain why matching text was mistaken for the entry point earlier; they cannot be added to the chain of arrows above. In particular, when two files both contain `request`, `header`, or similarly named entry points, ask "who actually calls whom?" before deciding whether to include them in the path.

It's best to organize the review notes around three locations: the local request/header section at the entry point, one direct caller, and the first actual consumer of gateway replay rotation. At each location, keep only the objects or call relationships that support the next hop. This avoids both overlooking `header envelope capture` and inventing a separate branch with no call edge just because it stands out. If the third location can still only be inferred from the name, leave it marked as awaiting confirmation; don't fill in the sketch with a speculative sequence.

v1 had only request.js and two relationships awaiting confirmation. Subsequent checks distinguished "a matching term appears in the file" from "the file actually participates in a call," and put `header envelope capture` back in its role as a location reference. The change was not to add more files, but to narrow the search from text hits to one direct caller, then require the next node to have an actual usage site. Ownership or internal processing that has not yet been confirmed remains outside this page's review scope.

If your investigation turns up a discrepancy in the package publication dry run, see `DOC-46`. That is a separate long-term record; it isn't the next stop after request-ingress, and it shouldn't be linked into this path diagram.

title: Postmortem: Package Publication Dry-Run Discrepancy

versions.body:
# Postmortem: Package Publication Dry-Run Discrepancy

During the package publication dry-run window, the visible results did not match what the original plan called for. What was visible initially was a discrepancy within the window, not a complete failure sufficient to point to a specific part of the publication logic. It was not recorded at the time as an error already present in the package contents; the only material retained was the visible results, a sanitized gateway event, and references to artifacts from the window that could still be rolled back.

The main impact was on verification. Before the window could proceed, the dry run could no longer be considered complete based only on the original plan; subsequent checks needed to use the artifacts retained at the time as their reference. No consumer-side results are recorded here, and the absence of those results was not taken to mean there was no impact.

## Window Log

- After execution of the original plan began, the first finding was that the visible results did not match expectations. At the time, the discrepancy was confirmed only within the dry-run window; it did not establish whether the cause lay in the input, the artifacts, or the publication steps.
- To avoid overwriting more clues as work continued, a sanitized gateway event was saved first. It was used to review the request shape, not as root-cause evidence; the sanitized content was also insufficient to reconstruct the full context.
- A control point was added during the interim recovery: record the last reversible package artifact. This meant that before continuing, it would at least be possible to return to the last package artifact in the window that could still be rolled back.
- After recovery, checks within the window could continue from that artifact reference. The record did not equate "window recovery" with "cause found"; those were different states at the time.

## Working Assessment at the Time

This postmortem retained the working assessment from the on-call shift: first treat the issue as a discrepancy in the publication dry-run window rather than jump to a root-cause conclusion about package publication. That assessment was useful at the time for deciding whether to pause and what to retain, but it did not explain why the visible results deviated from the original plan.

Even afterward, some people read "recovery" here as meaning that the package itself had been verified as correct. That was not what the original record meant. The interim recovery only established a single reversible point, reducing the risk of losing artifact references as the dry run continued; it did not replace separate checks of the gateway event, the publication process, or the final package contents.

## Still Unconfirmed

Unconfirmed: the stage at which the discrepancy first appeared, and whether there was a direct relationship between the saved event and the package artifact. Without sufficient material, the last reversible artifact should not be treated as the source of the failure, nor should this record be used to infer what external adopters had already received. If a follow-up review is needed, start with the retained artifacts and the window records from that time.
